sentence: [Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers](/welder-salary/) trail noticeably behind at every point BLS measures, a $53,750 median with a $77,530 top decile, roughly $30,700 below the structural ironworker 90th-percentile boundary despite a similar high school diploma entry bar and overlapping welding work on the job.
target_quote:
coreSummary: 'The median annual wage for welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers was $53,750 in May 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The bottom 10% earned less than $39,240 while the top 10% earned more than $77,530. BLS projects 2% employment growth from 2025 to 2035, slower than the roughly 3% average across all occupations, though about 40,300 openings are still projected each year.',
"SOC code 51-4121 is BLS's catch-all for welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers, defined as workers who use hand-held or remotely controlled equipment to join, repair, or cut metal parts and products. Roughly 437,700 people held these jobs in 2025, and BLS put the median annual wage at $53,750 that May, or $25.84 an hour. Pay ran from less than $39,240 at the 10th percentile to more than $77,530 at the 90th, a gap of roughly $38,290. That single wage figure covers all four job titles under the SOC code; BLS does not break out percentiles separately by specialty. For duties and safety on the job, see this site's guide to [what a welder does](/what-does-a-welder-do/).",
"That $53,750 figure folds together four separate job titles BLS tracks under one SOC code and tells apart by technique, not pay: welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers. BLS doesn't publish wage data for any of the four individually.",
answer: 'For May 2025, the annual midpoint for welders and the related cutting, soldering and brazing trades was $53,750, or $25.84 hourly. Half earned above that amount and half below, according to BLS.',
answer: 'The lower-decile boundary was $39,240 and the upper one $77,530 in May 2025, about $38,290 apart. Earnings were below the former for the bottom tenth and above the latter for the top tenth, for the combined four-title occupation.',
answer: 'A six-figure wage is above the $77,530 upper-decile boundary for May 2025 and would therefore be outside the lower 90% of this national distribution. The highest reported industry median was $59,440 for specialty contractors. Those figures do not set a maximum: the survey combines four broad job titles and supplies no separate estimate for specialized underwater or pipeline assignments.',
answer: "The decision depends on training cost, earnings expectations and working conditions. BLS describes a high-school entry route followed by technical and workplace training, generally quicker and cheaper than four years of college. Its $53,750 median trails several other trades requiring no bachelor's degree, and the 2% forecast through 2035 is below the roughly 3% national rate. Replacements still produce about 40,300 annual openings. Heat, noise, physical effort and outdoor weather also belong in that calculation; the pay distribution offers no personal guarantee or maximum.",

sentence: At the other extreme, [electrical power-line installers and repairers](/how-to-become-a-lineman/), commonly called linemen, post a $95,320 median well above any of the trades here, in a role whose path adds line-crew apprenticeship training and, usually, a CDL on top of the same nominal high school diploma bar.
target_quote:
coreSummary: "Per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, electrical power-line installers and repairers (SOC 49-9051) typically need only a high school diploma or equivalent to enter the occupation, building skills through long-term on-the-job training; apprenticeships are common. Two independently reviewed regional apprenticeship sponsors, Southwest Line Constructors and IBEW Local 1186's Hawaii training fund, both describe apprenticeship terms of roughly 7,000 hours of on-the-job training, spanning about three to four years depending on the sponsor, plus related classroom instruction; Southwest Line Constructors also requires a Class A commercial driver's license (CDL) to apply. BLS reports a median annual wage of $95,320 in May 2025, with the bottom 10% earning less than $51,470 and the top 10% earning more than $128,690.",
alt: 'Diagram showing the path to becoming a lineman: a high school diploma, meeting apprenticeship requirements including a commercial driver\'s license, roughly 7,000 hours of paid on-the-job apprenticeship training, and journeyman status, with a median pay of $95,320 a year per BLS.',
"BLS reports a median annual wage of $95,320 for electrical power-line installers and repairers in May 2025, or $45.83 an hour, well above the $50,980 median across all occupations that year. The bottom 10% earned less than $51,470, and the top 10% earned more than $128,690, a spread of more than $77,000, or more than 2.5 times, between the boundary figures BLS publishes.",
answer: 'The typical lineman took home $95,320 a year as of BLS\'s May 2025 release, close to $45.83 hourly. Pay ranged from under $51,470 at the low end of the scale to more than $128,690 at the top. Uncle Sam and the utility companies themselves paid the most, $111,900 and $103,060 respectively, while the firms BLS classifies under construction of utility systems paid the least of the five industries tracked, at $76,060.',
answer: "BLS tracks them as separate occupations with separate SOC codes, 49-9051 for this line-work role and 47-2111 for electricians, and lists electricians as a similar occupation on the lineman's BLS page. Both fields typically need nothing more than a standard high-school credential to get started, but linemen work on outdoor, high-voltage power-distribution lines, often at height, while [electricians](/how-to-become-an-electrician/) more often install and repair wiring and lower-voltage systems inside buildings. BLS's median pay for the two differs by about $32,000 a year, $95,320 for linemen versus $63,190 for electricians in May 2025, a gap the data does not explain beyond the setting and voltage differences it describes.",
